title: 42-storey tower proposed at Park and Victoria
subtitle: Affordable housing, parkland, traffic, privately owned public space, and the provincial appeal process were raised during the public hearing.
overview: The Planning and Strategic Initiatives Committee held a public hearing on a proposed 42-storey mixed-use building at 97-101 Park Street and 186-194 Victoria Street South. The committee recommended that Council adopt the Official Plan amendment and approve the zoning change {{vote:m1}}. The Official Plan amendment would then go to the Region of Waterloo for approval.

The proposal includes 436 homes, three ground-floor commercial units, and a publicly accessible plaza on Park Street. Staff said the site is in a major transit station area and that the project supports the city's intensification goals. A holding provision requires an updated urban design report and an updated traffic study before development can proceed. Parkland requirements will be met through a mix of credit for the public plaza and cash in lieu.

The applicant's representative said there is currently no proposal to contribute to affordable housing. Seven tenants in existing rental homes are to be offered relocation. Staff said the application's 90-day appeal period means Council must decide before July 25, 2023. Council will make the final decision.

decisions.item: Official Plan amendment, 97-101 Park St and 186-194 Victoria St S
decisions.detail: The committee recommended that Council adopt an amendment adding Special Policy Area 2 to allow a 42-storey mixed-use development, and forward it to the Region of Waterloo for approval {{vote:m1}}.

decisions.item: Zoning by-law amendment for the same lands
decisions.detail: The committee recommended approving the zoning change in the form attached to report DSD-2023-236, with a holding provision tied to urban design, traffic access, noise and site remediation matters.

debate: Delegates opposed to the proposal raised traffic. They cited accidents at Park and Victoria, the narrowing of Victoria Street, a nearby rail crossing, and drivers cutting through side streets. Staff replied that a traffic study found no major concerns, and that the Region required a holding provision for an updated study.

Opponents also objected to the height and shadows next to low-rise neighbourhoods, and to the lack of nearby park space. One delegate said Victoria Park is already crowded. Staff said the Park Central plan designates this corridor for high-intensity development, with heights stepping up toward downtown.

A neighbourhood association asked for at least 5% affordable units, larger setbacks for trees, more EV charging and more bike parking. The applicant's representative said no affordable housing contribution is proposed. Staff said inclusionary zoning is expected to be implemented in December. Staff also said the building would be set back 6.5 metres, with 296 bicycle spaces and 70 EV-ready parking spaces.

Councillors asked how privately owned public space stays open. Staff said a public easement would be registered on title, and the condominium corporation would be obliged to maintain it. One delegate spoke in support, citing the large family-sized units and the central location.

Several councillors criticized the appeal process for development decisions, citing the risk of costs at the Ontario Land Tribunal. One councillor said refusing such projects would be unpragmatic and that they would support this one. Another said they would let it pass but wanted more community benefits.
